Vladimir Nabokov. A Russian-American novelist and writer born in 1899, celebrated for his elaborate wordplay, psychological complexity, and experiments with form. His most famous novel, Lolita, scandalized readers with its unreliable narrator and baroque prose style, establishing him as a master of metafiction and linguistic innovation who influenced generations of postmodern writers.

Born in czarist Russia, Nabokov emigrated after the revolution, lived in Berlin and Paris before settling in America. His exile shaped his outsider perspective on language and belonging. He wrote Lolita in 1955, narrated by the predatory Humbert Humbert. The novel's formal brilliance and moral ambiguity made it a landmark of modern fiction despite initial scandal. Nabokov pioneered metafiction—novels about the act of writing itself, featuring characters aware of their fictionality and footnotes that undermine the text. His Pale Fire, published in 1962, is a novel disguised as a scholarly edition with a foreword, poem, and cranky commentary by an unreliable editor. He created intricate wordplay and multilingual puns. His prose is densely composed, demanding rereading. He considered himself a novelist of ideas, not ideas of a novelist. A lepidopterist, or butterfly collector, Nabokov wove scientific precision and taxonomic obsession into his literary aesthetics. He spent decades perfecting Pale Fire. James Joyce remains his great rival as a master of linguistic density and self-reflexive narrative in the modernist and postmodern canon. Nabokov synthesized high modernism with postmodern skepticism toward authorial presence, and influenced postmodern writers like Thomas Pynchon and David Foster Wallace.
